topics: 🐄🐑 New Mishna: Substituting Across Categories — herd for flock, male for female, blemished for unblemished
📖 The Doubled 'Good' — deriving that even good-for-good substitution is flogged
🔢 New Mishna: One for Two, Two for One — Rabbi Shimon's dissent
🔄 Substituting Twice for the Same Animal — Reish Lakish vs. Rabbi Yoḥanan on Rabbi Shimon's view
❓ Rabbi Avin's Unresolved Dilemmas — repeat substitution and the added fifth (ḥomesh)

overview.title: 📖 Overview: What Can Be Substituted, and How Many Times
overview.subtitle: Temurah 9a–9b
overview.hebrewSource: מְמִירִין מִן הַצֹּאן עַל הַבָּקָר, וּמִן הַבָּקָר עַל הַצֹּאן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Chapter Two opens with a mishna listing the category-crossings permitted (though still forbidden and flogged) in temurah: flock for herd, sheep for goats, male for female, unblemished for blemished — all derived from the verse's phrase 'animal for animal.' The Gemara analyzes the doubled word 'good' in the verse to derive two distinct rules: that substituting a good animal for a good one is still flogged, and that an animal blemished from birth can never be substituted for. A second mishna then debates whether one may substitute one animal for many (or many for one), with Rabbi Shimon restricting temurah to strictly one-for-one. The daf closes with Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yoḥanan's dispute over repeat substitution of the same consecrated animal, and a cluster of Rabbi Avin's dilemmas — all left as teiku — about substitution and the added one-fifth payment across chains of changed sanctity.

slides.title: 🐄🐑 What Categories Can Cross in Substitution
slides.subtitle: All derived from 'בְּהֵמָה בִּבְהֵמָה' — 'animal for animal' (Leviticus 27:10)

callout.label: Key distinction:
callout.text: 'Good for bad' works only when the blemish came after consecration; an animal blemished from the very start can never generate a valid temurah.

slides.title: 📖 Why Does the Verse Say 'Good' Twice?
slides.subtitle: Abaye and Rava each extract two separate rules from the repetition

lines.speaker: Question
lines.text: The verse could have said 'good for bad or bad for it' — why write 'for good' a second time?

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: The extra 'good' teaches: if the animal was good from the start, before consecration, one CAN substitute for it. If bad from the start, one cannot.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Both instances of 'good' are needed. One teaches that even good-for-good substitution is flogged; the other teaches the 'good/bad from the start' rule.

lines.speaker: Abaye's challenge
lines.text: Why do I need a verse for good-for-good? A kal vachomer suffices: if substituting a good animal for a bad one (an improvement!) is flogged, surely good-for-good is too!

lines.speaker: Rava's reply
lines.text: 'One does not administer punishment from a logical inference (קַל וָחוֹמֶר)' — lashes require an explicit verse, not mere logic.

callout.label: Principle at stake:
callout.text: Rava's rule — אֵין עוֹנְשִׁין מִן הַדִּין — that corporal punishment can never rest on logical inference alone, only on the Torah's explicit words.

slides.title: 🔢 New Mishna: One-for-Two, Two-for-One, or Strictly One-for-One?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Shimon dissents from the first tanna

boxes.title: First Tanna
items: One may substitute 1 for 2, 2 for 1, even 1 for 100 or 100 for 1
Source: 'בְּהֵמָה בִּבְהֵמָה' — a general term covering any number
'A group is also called behema' (cf. 'behema rabba,' Jonah 4:11)

boxes.title: Rabbi Shimon
items: Substitution works only strictly one animal for one animal
Source: 'וְהָיָה הוּא וּתְמוּרָתוֹ' — just as 'it' (הוּא) is singular, so is the substitute
A group is called 'behema rabba,' never plain 'behema' alone

callout.label: Note:
callout.text: Rabbi Shimon first argued from 'הוּא', but conceded his view could equally be derived from 'בְּהֵמָה בִּבְהֵמָה' once he saw how the Rabbis read that phrase.

slides.title: 🔄 Does Rabbi Shimon Allow Substituting Twice?
slides.subtitle: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yoḥanan disagree about the scope of his one-for-one rule

lines.speaker: Reish Lakish
lines.text: Rabbi Shimon does concede that one may substitute, and then substitute again, for the same consecrated animal — its original sanctity never went anywhere!

lines.speaker: Rabbi Yoḥanan
lines.text: No — just as Rabbi Shimon forbids substituting two animals for one at once, he equally forbids substituting twice in sequence for the same animal.

lines.speaker: Supporting baraitot
lines.text: Baraitot exist supporting each position — one explicitly barring repeat substitution, the other deriving from 'הוּא וּתְמוּרָתוֹ' that one may substitute even with a hundred animals in sequence.

callout.label: Unresolved tension:
callout.text: Both readings find textual support, leaving the precise boundary of Rabbi Shimon's 'one-for-one' rule genuinely contested.

slides.title: ❓ Rabbi Avin's Chain-of-Substitution Dilemmas
slides.subtitle: Each variant is tested and left as teiku

steps.content: 1️⃣ A guilt offering is substituted for once; it becomes blemished, its sanctity is transferred to a second animal — can THAT one be substituted for again?
2️⃣ Abaye sharpens the question: is the real variable 'two bodies, one sanctity' or 'one body, two sanctities'? Rabbi Avin says both matter together
3️⃣ Parallel question about the added ḥomesh (one-fifth): Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules only the ORIGINAL consecrator adds a fifth upon redemption, not one whose animal received transferred sanctity
4️⃣ Every combination of 'same body / different sanctity' and 'different body / same sanctity' is raised — and every one ends in תֵּיקוּ

callout.label: Why unresolved:
callout.text: These dilemmas probe exactly what 'the same act of substitution' means once an animal's sanctity has passed through several stages — a question the Gemara leaves open.

summary.principle: Substitution can cross species, sex, and blemish-status categories (but never for an animal blemished from birth), must generally be strictly one-for-one according to Rabbi Shimon, and the boundaries of 'repeat' substitution across chains of transferred sanctity remain unresolved.

flowSteps.content: 🐄🐑 Mishna: flock↔herd, sheep↔goats, male↔female, unblemished↔blemished all substitute — still flogged
📖 Doubled 'good' teaches: good-for-good is flogged too; congenital blemish never works

columns.content: 🔢 First tanna: any ratio (1-for-2, 100-for-1); R' Shimon: strictly 1-for-1
🔄 Does R' Shimon also bar substituting twice in sequence? Disputed

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: lashes require an explicit verse, never mere logical inference (אֵין עוֹנְשִׁין מִן הַדִּין)

quiz.q: According to the mishna, which type of blemished animal can NEVER be validly substituted for (or used as a substitute)?
o: Any blemished animal whatsoever
One that was blemished from birth, before it could have been consecrated unblemished
Only female blemished animals
Only blemished cattle
quiz.e: The mishna teaches that 'good for bad' substitution works only when the blemish came after consecration; an animal blemished from the very start cannot generate a valid temurah at all.

quiz.q: What is Rava's core objection to Abaye's attempt to derive 'good-for-good is flogged' through a kal vachomer (a fortiori inference)?
o: He says the inference is logically invalid
One does not administer punishment (lashes) based on a logical inference alone — אֵין עוֹנְשִׁין מִן הַדִּין
He says good-for-good substitution is actually permitted
He agrees entirely with Abaye
quiz.e: Rava's principle is that corporal punishment requires an explicit verse; a logical derivation, however compelling, cannot by itself generate liability for lashes.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Shimon in the second mishna, how must a substitution be structured?
o: Any number of animals may be substituted for any number of others
Strictly one non-sacred animal for one consecrated animal
Only females may be substituted
Only for guilt offerings
quiz.e: Rabbi Shimon derives from 'וְהָיָה הוּא וּתְמוּרָתוֹ' — since 'it' (הוּא) is singular — that the substitute must likewise be a single, specific animal, disputing the first tanna's allowance of any ratio.

quiz.q: What is the core disagreement between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yoḥanan regarding Rabbi Shimon's opinion?
o: Whether Rabbi Shimon permits any substitution at all
Whether Rabbi Shimon, who bars substituting two animals for one, also bars substituting twice in sequence for the same animal
Whether Rabbi Shimon agrees with the first tanna entirely
Whether Rabbi Shimon applies only to blemished animals
quiz.e: Reish Lakish holds Rabbi Shimon permits sequential substitution for the same consecrated animal (its sanctity never left), while Rabbi Yoḥanan holds he forbids it, just as he forbids substituting two-for-one.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who must add the extra one-fifth (ḥomesh) upon redeeming a blemished consecrated animal?
o: Anyone who redeems any consecrated item
Only the one who directly consecrated it originally (מַקְדִּישׁ), not one whose animal received transferred sanctity (מַתְפִּיס)
Only priests
No one is ever required to add a fifth
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives from 'and if he who consecrated it will redeem' that the added fifth applies only to the original consecrator, not to someone whose animal became holy through a transfer of sanctity (like a substitute).
